chapters.customSummary:
- A join stitches tables back together through FK-to-PK matches, and the join type decides what happens to unmatched rows.
- Use aliases and alias.column; ambiguous columns raise an error (MySQL 1052).
- INNER JOIN keeps matched rows only and silently hides the rest (5 of 7 employees; 10 of 11 leave requests). Compare base-table row counts with joined row counts.
- LEFT JOIN keeps every left row with NULLs on no match; anti-join (LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS) finds orphans and missing data; avoid NOT IN with nullable columns.
- Left join from the parent side finds parents with no children; use COUNT(child.id), not COUNT(*), or empty groups show 1.
- WHERE vs ON: right-table conditions in WHERE turn a LEFT JOIN into an inner join; put match conditions in ON. Test that empty categories still show with zeros.
- RIGHT JOIN is a mirrored left join, best rewritten; FULL JOIN keeps both sides (not in MySQL, use left + right with UNION ALL) and is the tool for comparing two datasets; CROSS JOIN gives every combination (28 rows), and a forgotten WHERE in comma syntax makes an accidental one.
- Multi-table joins: choose inner for mandatory relationships, left for optional (approver); an inner join after a left join can undo it.
- ON can use several columns and ranges (e.g., punches during approved leave); NULL never matches NULL (use <=> or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM).
- Fan-out: one-to-many joins multiply rows and inflate counts/sums (QA counted 8 vs real 3); compare with single-table totals and use COUNT(DISTINCT ...).
- USING/NATURAL JOIN differ by dialect (no USING in SQL Server) and NATURAL is risky; *= and (+) are obsolete syntax.
- InnoDB auto-indexes FKs; PostgreSQL and SQL Server don't, which can slow joins and parent deletes.
- Automation: compare UI rows with a join query (requirement-driven, e.g., dash for missing approver); missing rows in the UI usually mean an inner join dropped them.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Why joins exist at all
A relational database stores each fact once. An employee's department name lives in departments, and the employee row stores only the department's ID. But the screen you're testing shows "Asha Karki, QA" in one row, so somebody has to stitch the two tables back together at query time. That stitching is a join. Nearly every screen, report, export and API response in the HRMS is the result of at least one join, so nearly every DB-side check you write for them needs one too.
The anatomy of a join
```sql
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, d.name AS department
FROM   employees e
JOIN   departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id;
```

Four parts matter. employees e gives the table a short alias, e. JOIN departments d names the second table. ON d.department_id = e.department_id is the join condition, which says which rows belong together (a foreign key matched to a primary key, in almost every case). And columns are written as alias.column, because both tables may have a column with the same name:
MySQL:      ERROR 1052 (23000): Column 'department_id' in field list is ambiguous
PostgreSQL: ERROR: column reference "department_id" is ambiguous
SQL Server: Ambiguous column name 'department_id'.

Conceptually, the database takes each row from the left table, looks for rows in the right table where the ON condition is true, and emits one combined row for every match. The join type decides only one thing: what happens to rows that find no partner. That is where nearly all tester-relevant behaviour lives.
## A useful analogy from UI testing
A foreign key is like an HTML for="email-input" on a label or an aria-labelledby on an element. It's a reference to another element's ID. A join follows the reference. An orphan row is the database equivalent of a for attribute pointing at an ID that doesn't exist in the page, which is a dangling reference nobody notices until something depends on it.
## INNER JOIN: only rows with a partner on both sides
JOIN on its own means INNER JOIN. It keeps a combined row only when the ON condition finds a match, and silently drops everything else.
```sql
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, d.name AS department
FROM   employees e
INNER JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
ORDER  BY e.employee_id;
```

| employee_id \| first_name \| department | 1           \| Asha       \| QA | 2           \| Ravi       \| QA |
|---|---|---|
| 3           \| Mina       \| Finance | 4           \| Sita       \| HR | 5           \| Bikash     \| QA |

There are seven employees but only five result rows. Puja (department NULL) and Tenzing (department 9, which doesn't exist) vanished with no error and no warning. That is the single most important thing about INNER JOIN for a tester: it hides unmatched rows. If a report is built on an inner join, then any employee with a broken department reference simply doesn't appear in the report, and nobody ever sees a failure. Compare the two numbers to see it:
```sql
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM leave_requests) AS leave_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM leave_requests lr
        JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = lr.employee_id) AS joined_rows;
```

leave_rows | joined_rows
11         | 10

Eleven leave requests exist, but a screen that inner-joins to employees can show only ten. The missing one is the orphan pointing at employee 99. Whether that's acceptable is a requirement question (should a request with a broken employee reference be visible, flagged or impossible?), but you can only ask it if you noticed the gap. Comparing "rows in the base table" with "rows after the join" is one of the quickest checks in this manual.
## LEFT JOIN: keep every row from the left table
LEFT JOIN (also written LEFT OUTER JOIN) keeps all rows from the left table. When there's no match on the right, the right-hand columns are filled with NULL.
```sql
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.department_id, d.name AS department
FROM   employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
ORDER  BY e.employee_id;
```

| employee_id \| first_name \| department_id \| department | 1           \| Asha       \| 2             \| QA | 2           \| Ravi       \| 2             \| QA | 3           \| Mina       \| 1             \| Finance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4           \| Sita       \| 3             \| HR | 5           \| Bikash     \| 2             \| QA | 6           \| Puja       \| NULL          \| NULL | 7           \| Tenzing    \| 9             \| NULL |

All seven employees are back. Puja and Tenzing both show NULL for department, but for different reasons: Puja has no department assigned (probably legitimate), while Tenzing points at department 9, which doesn't exist (definitely a defect). The department column looks identical for both, which is why you must look at the left-side foreign key too, as this section's next pattern does.
## The anti-join: LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL finds what's missing
If you LEFT JOIN and then filter for rows where the right side's key is NULL, you get exactly the left rows that have no match. This "anti-join" is the workhorse for finding orphans, unassigned records and "things that should exist but don't."
```sql
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.department_id
FROM   employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
WHERE  d.department_id IS NULL;
```

employee_id | first_name | department_id
6           | Puja       | NULL
7           | Tenzing    | 9

To isolate only the real orphan (a filled foreign key with no parent), add the condition that the foreign key itself isn't null:
## WHERE  e.department_id IS NOT NULL AND d.department_id IS NULL;   -- Tenzing only

Test the right-hand side's primary key for NULL (d.department_id IS NULL), not a column that could legitimately be null in a matched row. The same result can be written with NOT EXISTS, which is safe against NULL traps:

| SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name | FROM   employees e |
|---|---|
| WHERE  e.department_id IS NOT NULL | AND  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM departments d WHERE d.department_id = e.department_id); |

Avoid NOT IN (SELECT ...) here whenever the subquery column might contain NULL, for the reason explained in 2.3. Chapter 4.3 builds full orphan-detection on these patterns.
## LEFT JOIN from the "one" side: parents with no children
Flip the direction and the same idea finds parents that have no children. Departments with staff counts:
```sql
SELECT d.name,
```
| COUNT(*)             AS count_star, | COUNT(e.employee_id) AS staff | FROM   departments d |
|---|---|---|
| LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id | GROUP  BY d.department_id, d.name | ORDER  BY d.department_id; |

name    | count_star | staff
| Finance \| 1          \| 1 | QA      \| 3          \| 3 |
|---|---|
| HR      \| 1          \| 1 | Legal   \| 1          \| 0 |

Legal has nobody, but COUNT(*) reports 1, because the outer join produced one row (with NULL employee columns) and COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(e.employee_id) counts only non-NULL values and correctly reports 0. This is the classic wrong-count bug from 3.1, and you'll find it in real report code too. A dashboard tile "Employees per department" that shows 1 for an empty department is this exact defect.
## WHERE versus ON in outer joins
For inner joins it makes no difference whether an extra condition sits in ON or in WHERE. For outer joins it changes the result. Consider "each department and its active staff count":
-- Condition in ON: filters the right side BEFORE the join, keeps every department
```sql
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.employee_id) AS active_staff
FROM   departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id AND e.status = 'active'
GROUP  BY d.department_id, d.name ORDER BY d.department_id;
```

name    | active_staff
| Finance \| 1 | QA      \| 2 |
|---|---|
| HR      \| 0 | Legal   \| 0 |

-- Condition in WHERE: filters AFTER the join, wipes out the unmatched (NULL) rows
```sql
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.employee_id) AS active_staff
```
| FROM   departments d | LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id |
|---|---|
| WHERE  e.status = 'active' | GROUP  BY d.department_id, d.name ORDER BY d.department_id; |

name    | active_staff
Finance | 1
QA      | 2

HR and Legal are gone, because for them e.status is NULL (HR's only employee, Sita, is resigned) and NULL = 'active' isn't true. Putting a condition on the right-hand table in WHERE quietly turns a LEFT JOIN back into an INNER JOIN. The rule: conditions that describe which right-side rows may match go in ON; conditions that filter the final result go in WHERE. When a report is "missing" empty categories (a department, a leave type, a month with zero activity), this mistake is the first suspect, and it's a perfect test scenario: create a category with no data and check the UI still lists it with a zero.
## RIGHT JOIN: LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped
RIGHT JOIN keeps every row from the right table. A RIGHT JOIN B returns the same rows as B LEFT JOIN A.
```sql
SELECT e.first_name, d.name AS department
FROM   employees e
RIGHT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id;
```

That returns six rows: the five matched employees plus Legal with a NULL first name. Puja and Tenzing don't appear, because the right table (departments) is the one being preserved. Most teams avoid RIGHT JOIN and rewrite as LEFT JOIN with tables in the other order, because reading left to right with "keep the first table" is easier. You still need to recognise it in legacy queries and in ORM-generated SQL.
## FULL OUTER JOIN: keep everything from both sides
FULL JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both tables: employees with no department, departments with no employees, and every matched pair.
```sql
-- PostgreSQL / SQL Server
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, d.department_id, d.name AS department
FROM   employees e
FULL OUTER JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id;
```

The result is 8 rows: 5 matched, plus Puja and Tenzing (no department), plus Legal (no employees). MySQL has no FULL JOIN. The standard workaround is a left join, then unmatched right rows added on:
```sql
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, d.department_id, d.name AS department
FROM   employees e LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
UNION ALL
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, d.department_id, d.name
FROM   employees e RIGHT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
WHERE  e.employee_id IS NULL;
```

(The UNION and UNION ALL operators are covered in 5.4.) A full join is the ideal tool for comparing two data sets: rows on the left only are "missing from the right," rows on the right only are "unexpected extras," and matched rows can be compared column by column. That's the backbone of expected-versus-actual checking in 6.2 and migration validation in 6.1.
## CROSS JOIN: every combination
A cross join has no ON condition and pairs every left row with every right row: 7 employees × 4 departments = 28 rows.
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees CROSS JOIN departments;   -- 28
```

It has legitimate uses (generating every employee-by-month combination to find missing rows, or building test data), but it's more often an accident. The accident usually looks like this:
-- Old comma syntax with the WHERE forgotten: returns 28 rows instead of 5
```sql
SELECT e.first_name, d.name FROM employees e, departments d;
```

The comma style (FROM a, b WHERE a.id = b.id) is legal and you'll see it in old code, but forgetting the WHERE gives a cartesian product. A report suddenly showing thousands of rows or a page that times out after someone "just added a join" is a cross join in disguise.
## Joining several tables
Real screens join three or four tables. Join them one at a time; each JOIN builds on the result so far. Here is the leave request list as an approver would see it, with the requester, the leave type and the approver (the same employees table twice, under two aliases, which 4.2 explains):

| SELECT lr.leave_request_id, | CONCAT(e.first_name, ' ', e.last_name)  AS employee, | lt.name                                 AS leave_type, | lr.days, lr.status, | CONCAT(a.first_name, ' ', a.last_name)  AS approver |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FROM   leave_requests lr | JOIN   employees   e  ON e.employee_id   = lr.employee_id | JOIN   leave_types lt ON lt.leave_type_id = lr.leave_type_id | LEFT JOIN employees a ON a.employee_id   = lr.approved_by | ORDER  BY lr.leave_request_id; |

leave_request_id | employee      | leave_type | days | status   | approver
| 1                \| Ravi Shrestha \| Annual     \| 3    \| pending  \| NULL | 2                \| Asha Karki    \| Sick       \| 1    \| approved \| Mina Thapa | 3                \| Ravi Shrestha \| Sick       \| 2    \| rejected \| Asha Karki | 4                \| Mina Thapa    \| Annual     \| 6    \| pending  \| NULL | 5                \| Asha Karki    \| Annual     \| 3    \| approved \| Mina Thapa |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6                \| Ravi Shrestha \| Sick       \| 1    \| approved \| Asha Karki | 7                \| Ravi Shrestha \| Sick       \| 2    \| approved \| Asha Karki | 8                \| Mina Thapa    \| Sick       \| 2    \| approved \| Asha Karki | 9                \| Asha Karki    \| Sick       \| 2    \| pending  \| NULL | 11               \| Bikash Rai    \| Annual     \| 2    \| pending  \| NULL |

The choice of join type for each relationship encodes a requirement. The requester and leave type are mandatory (inner joins), while the approver is optional (a left join, because pending requests have none). Request 10 is missing because employee 99 doesn't exist. A classic mistake is to make the approver join an INNER JOIN, which silently deletes every pending request from the list, exactly the requests an approver most needs to see. If the UI's "Pending" tab is empty while the table has pending rows, check for this.
A related trap: an INNER JOIN placed after a LEFT JOIN can undo it. If you LEFT JOIN the approver and then JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = a.department_id, the rows where the approver is NULL can't match a department and get dropped again. Chain optional relationships with LEFT JOIN all the way down.
## Joins with more than one column, and non-equality joins
The ON condition can combine several tests. It can also use ranges instead of equality, which is essential for date-based rules. Here's a check for employees who have attendance punches on a day they had approved leave:
```sql
SELECT a.employee_id, a.work_date, a.check_in, lr.leave_request_id
```
| FROM   attendance a | JOIN   leave_requests lr | ON  lr.employee_id = a.employee_id |
|---|---|---|
| AND lr.status = 'approved' | AND a.work_date BETWEEN lr.start_date AND lr.end_date | WHERE  a.check_in IS NOT NULL; |

(0 rows)

Zero rows means the check passes. Employee 1's approved leave on 15 Sep has an attendance row, but with no punches (the check_in IS NOT NULL filter excludes it). If the app had let that employee check in on the leave day, this query would return the row, which is a real cross-module rule (Attendance versus Leave) worth testing on every release. Chapter 10.4 expands it.
## NULL never joins to NULL
NULL = NULL isn't true (2.3), so two rows whose join columns are both NULL do not match. That's why Puja's NULL department joins to nothing. If you truly need NULLs to match (comparing two datasets where blank equals blank), use a null-safe comparison: a.col <=> b.col in MySQL, or a.col IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.col in PostgreSQL and SQL Server 2022 and later.
## Row multiplication (fan-out) and how to catch it
A join produces one output row per matching pair. If one employee has four leave requests, joining employees to leave requests yields four rows for that employee. Any count or sum computed afterwards is then inflated:

| SELECT d.name, | COUNT(*)                     AS wrong_count, | COUNT(DISTINCT e.employee_id) AS real_count | FROM   departments d |
|---|---|---|---|
| JOIN   employees e       ON e.department_id = d.department_id | JOIN   leave_requests lr ON lr.employee_id  = e.employee_id | GROUP  BY d.name | ORDER  BY d.name; |

name    | wrong_count | real_count
Finance | 2           | 1
## QA      | 8           | 3

QA has three employees, but the join produced 8 rows (Asha 3 requests, Ravi 4, Bikash 1). HR is missing altogether, because Sita has no leave requests and it's an inner join. Both numbers can look plausible in isolation. The defence is a habit: after any join that feeds a count or sum, compare with the plain single-table number (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees and so on). If a payroll or leave report over-counts, one-to-many fan-out is the usual culprit. The same defect causes duplicate rows in a UI list, when the join column of the "one" side isn't actually unique (a lookup table with two rows for the same code).
## USING, NATURAL JOIN and old syntax
When both tables have a join column with the same name, MySQL and PostgreSQL allow JOIN departments USING (department_id), a shorthand that also merges the two columns into one in the output. SQL Server doesn't support USING. NATURAL JOIN automatically joins on every column name the tables share, which is dangerous, since adding a created_at column to both tables silently changes the join. Avoid it. Very old SQL Server and Oracle code uses *= or (+) for outer joins, which is obsolete syntax you may only meet in legacy stored procedures.
## Joins and indexes
Joins are fast when the join columns are indexed. MySQL's InnoDB automatically creates an index on every foreign key column. PostgreSQL and SQL Server do not, so a child table with an un-indexed foreign key can make a join (and a parent delete, which has to check for children) very slow as data grows. If a joined report is slow only in a large environment, mention this when you escalate (8.5).
## Verifying joined screens from automation
A list screen that shows names from several tables is a joined result set. Compare it row by row with an equivalent query. Note that the test below asserts a requirement (pending requests must show a dash for approver), not just whatever the query returns:
```ts
test('leave request list shows employee, type and approver from DB', async ({ page }) => {
| await page.goto('/leave/requests'); | const uiRows = await page.locator('table#leave tbody tr').evaluateAll(trs => | trs.map(tr => { | const td = tr.querySelectorAll('td'); | return { |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| id: Number(td[0].textContent), | employee: td[1].textContent!.trim(), | approver: td[5].textContent!.trim(), | }; | })); |
```

```ts
  const [rows]: any = await db.execute(`
    SELECT lr.leave_request_id AS id,
| CONCAT(e.first_name, ' ', e.last_name) AS employee, | COALESCE(CONCAT(a.first_name, ' ', a.last_name), '—') AS approver | FROM   leave_requests lr |
|---|---|---|
| JOIN   employees e ON e.employee_id = lr.employee_id | LEFT JOIN employees a ON a.employee_id = lr.approved_by | ORDER  BY lr.leave_request_id`); |
```

  expect(uiRows).toEqual(rows);
});

If the UI list drops a row that the database has (like request 10, hidden by an inner join), the comparison fails, and that difference is your finding. The equivalent Selenium version reads the same cells with driver.find_elements(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "table#leave tbody tr") and compares against a pymysql cursor.

| Which join for which job | You want to know... | Use | Rows that have a partner in both tables | INNER JOIN |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Every row of A, with B's data when it exists | LEFT JOIN | Rows of A that have no partner in B (orphans, missing data) | LEFT JOIN ... WHERE b.key IS NULL (or NOT EXISTS) | Every row of both, matched where possible |
| FULL OUTER JOIN (MySQL: UNION workaround) | Every combination | CROSS JOIN | The same table related to itself | Self join (4.2) |

For our tables the row counts come out as: INNER 5, LEFT (employees first) 7, RIGHT 6, FULL 8, CROSS 28. If your counts differ from a join you expected to behave a certain way, that's the first clue that unmatched rows are being kept or dropped unexpectedly.

chapters.title: 4.2 Self Joins
chapters.overviewText: A self join isn't a separate join type. It is any join where both sides are the same table, distinguished by aliases. It works whenever rows in a table refer to other rows in the same table, or whenever you need to compare a row with its siblings. In our schema, employees.manager_id points at employees.employee_id, so each row is potentially both an employee and someone else's manager. The aliases give the two roles different names, and they're mandatory, because without them the database can't tell which copy of first_name you mean. Read it as: e is the employee, m is the row that e.manager_id points to. The analogy in UI automation is an element and its parent. Selenium's element.find_elem
chapters.why: 4.2 Self Joins is how a tester proves stored state, not just the screen. A self join isn't a separate join type.
chapters.when: Open this chapter when you are on the Joins path and need Self Joins against the hrms_practice schema, a shared QA database, or a Bizlevate HRMS screen.

practical.scenario: A leave, payroll, attendance, or appointment check depends on Self Joins.
practical.pass: You apply Self Joins on the sample database (or a tagged QA row) and can say what empty vs non-empty results mean.
practical.fail: You copy a blog query, skip Self Joins, or treat a UI success toast as proof the row is correct.

chapters.customSummary:
- Same table on both sides with mandatory aliases; think "element vs its parent."
- Employee to manager (LEFT JOIN to keep top-level people); reverse it for direct-report counts, and note raw counts vs the UI's soft-delete rule (2 vs 1 for Asha).
- Violation queries: self-manager, reports under inactive/resigned/deleted managers (offboarding test), mutual managers; all should return zero rows.
- Pairs with the same value use a.id < b.id to avoid mirrored duplicates and self-pairs; also finds duplicates that a unique constraint misses.
- Overlap detection: a.start <= b.end AND b.start <= a.end with a.id < b.id, filtered to active statuses; use strict < for time slots; test adjacent, one-day-shared, contained and identical ranges.
- Recursive CTE walks a hierarchy of any depth (preview of 5.2); if its row count is smaller than the table, the missing rows are in a cycle.
- Consecutive-row comparisons are better with LAG/LEAD (5.5).
- Typical uses: manager/approver lookup, org charts, delegation chains, overlapping ranges, duplicate and consecutive-record checks.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## A table joined to itself
A self join isn't a separate join type. It is any join where both sides are the same table, distinguished by aliases. It works whenever rows in a table refer to other rows in the same table, or whenever you need to compare a row with its siblings. In our schema, employees.manager_id points at employees.employee_id, so each row is potentially both an employee and someone else's manager. The aliases give the two roles different names, and they're mandatory, because without them the database can't tell which copy of first_name you mean.

| SELECT e.employee_id, | e.first_name AS employee, | m.first_name AS manager |
|---|---|---|
| FROM   employees e | LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id | ORDER  BY e.employee_id; |

| employee_id \| employee \| manager | 1           \| Asha     \| NULL | 2           \| Ravi     \| Asha | 3           \| Mina     \| NULL |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4           \| Sita     \| NULL | 5           \| Bikash   \| Asha | 6           \| Puja     \| NULL | 7           \| Tenzing  \| Ravi |

Read it as: e is the employee, m is the row that e.manager_id points to. The analogy in UI automation is an element and its parent. Selenium's element.find_element(By.XPATH, "..") and Playwright's locator.locator('..') do the same thing in the DOM. With LEFT JOIN, employees with no manager still appear (with NULL); with INNER JOIN only the three employees who report to someone (Ravi, Bikash, Tenzing) would be returned. Choose based on whether "no manager" is a valid state for the screen you're testing.
## Direct reports per manager
Reverse the roles and you get a team-size report. The version with the soft-delete rule shows why "the number on screen" and "the number in the table" can legitimately differ:
```sql
SELECT m.first_name AS manager,
```
| COUNT(*)                                        AS all_reports, | SUM(CASE WHEN e.is_deleted = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS visible_reports | FROM   employees m |
|---|---|---|
| JOIN   employees e ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id | GROUP  BY m.employee_id, m.first_name | ORDER  BY m.employee_id; |

manager | all_reports | visible_reports
Asha    | 2           | 1
## Ravi    | 1           | 1

Asha manages Ravi and Bikash, but Bikash is soft-deleted, so a "My Team" screen should show one person, not two. Testers often see a raw count and a UI count disagree and file it as a bug, when the actual defect (if any) is whether the UI's number follows the documented rule. Confirm the requirement, then write the query that implements it. The corresponding UI check compares the names on the "My Team" page with SELECT first_name FROM employees WHERE manager_id = ? AND is_deleted = 0 ORDER BY first_name.
## Finding hierarchy violations
Because the relationship is inside one table, the foreign key can't stop logically wrong data. These are classic violation queries (empty result means the data is fine):
-- 1. Someone is their own manager
```sql
SELECT employee_id, first_name FROM employees WHERE manager_id = employee_id;
```

-- 2. Reports whose manager is inactive, resigned or deleted
```sql
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name AS employee, m.first_name AS manager, m.status, m.is_deleted
FROM   employees e
JOIN   employees m ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
WHERE  m.status <> 'active' OR m.is_deleted = 1;
```

-- 3. Two people who manage each other
```sql
SELECT a.employee_id AS emp_a, b.employee_id AS emp_b
FROM   employees a
JOIN   employees b ON a.manager_id = b.employee_id AND b.manager_id = a.employee_id
WHERE  a.employee_id < b.employee_id;
```

On our data all three return no rows. They earn their place in a regression suite because of what workflows can do to them. The second one is the offboarding test: after you mark Asha as resigned in the app, does the app reassign Ravi and Bikash, block the resignation, or leave two employees reporting to a person who no longer works there? The result set after the workflow tells you which happened. That matters for approval flows too, because leave requests routed "to the manager" go nowhere if the manager is inactive (10.5).
## Colleagues who share a manager (pairs)
To relate rows to other rows with the same value, join a table to itself on that value and avoid mirrored duplicates with <:
```sql
SELECT a.first_name AS person_a, b.first_name AS person_b, a.manager_id
FROM   employees a
JOIN   employees b ON a.manager_id = b.manager_id
                  AND a.employee_id < b.employee_id;
```

person_a | person_b | manager_id
## Ravi     | Bikash   | 1

Without the a.employee_id < b.employee_id condition, every pair appears twice (Ravi/Bikash and Bikash/Ravi) and every person also pairs with themselves. The < trick keeps each pair once. Also note that the three managerless employees are not paired with each other, because NULL = NULL isn't true. This is the same idea that finds duplicate records that a unique constraint would miss, for example two employees with the same name and hire date but different IDs:
```sql
SELECT a.employee_id, b.employee_id, a.first_name, a.last_name, a.hire_date
FROM   employees a
JOIN   employees b ON a.first_name = b.first_name AND a.last_name = b.last_name
                  AND a.hire_date = b.hire_date AND a.employee_id < b.employee_id;
```

(GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 from 3.2 finds the same duplicates. The self join has the advantage of returning both IDs side by side, which is exactly what a bug report needs.)
## Overlap detection: the most valuable self join for testers
Two ranges overlap if each starts before the other ends. Comparing a table's rows with its own other rows this way finds double-booked leave, overlapping shifts and clashing appointments.
```sql
SELECT a.leave_request_id AS req_a, b.leave_request_id AS req_b,
```
| a.employee_id, a.start_date AS a_start, a.end_date AS a_end, | b.start_date AS b_start, b.end_date AS b_end | FROM   leave_requests a | JOIN   leave_requests b | ON  a.employee_id = b.employee_id |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AND a.leave_request_id < b.leave_request_id | AND a.start_date <= b.end_date | AND b.start_date <= a.end_date | WHERE  a.status IN ('pending', 'approved') | AND  b.status IN ('pending', 'approved'); |

(0 rows)

No employee currently has overlapping active requests. To see the query bite, imagine Ravi's pending request 1 (5 to 7 Oct) and a new request from 6 to 8 Oct: the result would contain req_a = 1, req_b = 12 and you'd know the app allowed a double booking. Three details matter. The IN ('pending','approved') filter excludes rejected and cancelled requests, since those don't block anything. The comparison is inclusive (<=) for date-only leave, where two requests sharing a single day do overlap. For appointments with times, use strict <, because a booking ending at 10:00 and another starting at 10:00 do not clash. And the boundary cases to test in the UI are exactly the ones this query encodes: adjacent ranges, sharing one day, one range fully inside another, and identical ranges.
## Hierarchies of unknown depth: a first look at recursive CTEs
A self join walks one level. To walk the entire reporting chain (manager, manager's manager, and so on) you'd need one join per level, which doesn't scale. The general answer is a recursive query, previewed here and covered properly in 5.2:
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    SELECT employee_id, first_name, manager_id, 1 AS level
```
| FROM   employees | WHERE  manager_id IS NULL |
|---|---|
| UNION ALL | SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.manager_id, o.level + 1 |
| FROM   employees e | JOIN   org o ON e.manager_id = o.employee_id |
| ) | SELECT employee_id, first_name, level FROM org ORDER BY level, employee_id; |

| employee_id \| first_name \| level | 1           \| Asha       \| 1 | 3           \| Mina       \| 1 | 4           \| Sita       \| 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6           \| Puja       \| 1 | 2           \| Ravi       \| 2 | 5           \| Bikash     \| 2 | 7           \| Tenzing    \| 3 |

(SQL Server writes WITH org AS (...) without the word RECURSIVE.) This gives you the expected depth of every person, so you can check an org-chart screen or an approval chain of "up to three levels." It also detects cycles as a side effect. Someone in a loop (A manages B, B manages A) is never reachable from a top-level employee, so they're missing from this result. If COUNT(*) of the result is smaller than COUNT(*) of employees, the difference is people trapped in a cycle. That test finds cycles the simple "two people managing each other" query above can't, such as a three-person loop.
## Comparing a row with the previous row
Self joins also compare consecutive rows, for instance "each attendance day versus the same employee's previous day," by joining on b.work_date = a.work_date - INTERVAL 1 DAY. Modern SQL does this more cleanly with the window functions LAG and LEAD (5.5), so treat the self join as the fallback for databases or teams that avoid them.
## Where self joins show up in the HRMS
Manager and approver lookups, team and org-chart screens, delegation chains, referral chains ("referred by another employee"), overlapping-range rules (leave, shifts, appointments), duplicate detection, and consecutive-record checks. If a table has a column that points back at its own primary key, or a rule that says "no two rows of the same kind may collide," a self join is how you verify it.

chapters.why: 4.3 Practical QA Scenario: Validating Foreign Key Relationships is how a tester proves stored state, not just the screen. A foreign key (FK) is a database-enforced rule: the value in the child column must exist as a key in the parent table (or be NULL, if the column allows it).
chapters.when: Open this chapter when you are on the Joins path and need Practical QA Scenario: Validating Foreign Key Relationships against the hrms_practice schema, a shared QA database, or a Bizlevate HRMS screen.

practical.scenario: A leave, payroll, attendance, or appointment check depends on Practical QA Scenario: Validating Foreign Key Relationships.
practical.pass: You apply Practical QA Scenario: Validating Foreign Key Relationships on the sample database (or a tagged QA row) and can say what empty vs non-empty results mean.
practical.fail: You copy a blog query, skip Practical QA Scenario: Validating Foreign Key Relationships, or treat a UI success toast as proof the row is correct.

chapters.customSummary:
- FKs can be missing, disabled during loads (re-enabling doesn't revalidate), untrusted (NOT VALID, is_not_trusted), impossible across boundaries, or satisfied by a soft-deleted parent (logical orphan).
- Step 1: list the FKs via information_schema (MySQL), pg_constraint (convalidated), sys.foreign_keys (is_disabled, is_not_trusted), and check @@foreign_key_checks; compare with the design and look for FK-shaped columns without constraints (naming heuristics miss things like approved_by).
- Step 2: an anti-join scoreboard, one UNION ALL line per relationship, gives orphan counts (3 planted orphans found); guard nullable FKs with IS NOT NULL; list actual rows for bug reports.
- Step 3: logical orphans (pending leave for inactive/deleted employees, payroll for resigned staff, approver rules) need hand-written checks.
- Step 4: completeness checks find missing children (active employees without August payroll); put the month condition in ON and confirm business rules (hire date, proration).
- Step 5: cardinality checks (one payroll row per employee per month) expose duplicates; recommend a UNIQUE constraint alongside the data fix.
- Step 6: behaviour tests inside a rolled-back transaction: bad child insert (MySQL 1452 / PG / SQL Server 547) and parent delete (MySQL 1451); know the referential actions (RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT) and verify UI/API give friendly errors, not raw ones or surprise cascades; assert on deltas in shared databases.
- Step 7: for soft deletes, the app must clean up children, so re-run logical-orphan queries after offboarding/status changes.
- Step 8: keep everything as a reusable suite run after migrations, imports, refreshes and releases (9.4, 10.2).
- Integrity bug report: relationship, query, count and sample IDs, environment/time, likely cause, visible impact, CSV attachment (11.3); severity depends on what the data feeds.
- Cleanup script removes Part 4's planted rows (preview first, delete by ID); auto-increment values won't reset.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## What a foreign key promises, and where the promise breaks
A foreign key (FK) is a database-enforced rule: the value in the child column must exist as a key in the parent table (or be NULL, if the column allows it). When it works, an orphan row is impossible. But the promise depends on conditions that are easy to break, and every one of them is a scenario you can test:
The constraint was never created. Many real schemas have employee_id columns with no FK at all, because a developer skipped it or the table was created by a script.
The constraint was disabled during a load. Migrations and imports often turn checks off for speed. In MySQL that's SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 0; in SQL Server, ALTER TABLE ... NOCHECK CONSTRAINT; in PostgreSQL, session_replication_role = replica or disabling triggers. Re-enabling does not re-validate rows already loaded, so orphans inserted while checks were off stay forever. That is how our sample orphans got in.
The constraint exists but isn't trusted. PostgreSQL's NOT VALID and SQL Server's untrusted (is_not_trusted = 1) constraints enforce the rule only for new rows.
The reference crosses a boundary the database can't check: another database, another service, or a "polymorphic" column like entity_type plus entity_id.
The parent is "gone" without being deleted. Soft deletes (is_deleted = 1) leave the parent row in place, so the FK is satisfied, but a child now belongs to something the app treats as nonexistent. This is a logical orphan, and no constraint can catch it.
Your job is to test all five: verify the constraints exist, verify they are enforced, and independently query for the rows that should be impossible.
## Step 1: check which foreign keys exist
Ask the database which relationships it actually enforces, then compare with the design (or with the ER diagram in Appendix E).
```sql
-- MySQL
SELECT table_name, column_name, constraint_name, referenced_table_name, referenced_column_name
FROM   information_schema.key_column_usage
WHERE  table_schema = 'hrms_practice' AND referenced_table_name IS NOT NULL
ORDER  BY table_name, column_name;
```

table_name     | column_name   | constraint_name    | referenced_table_name | referenced_column_name
## attendance     | employee_id   | attendance_ibfk_1  | employees             | employee_id
employees      | department_id | employees_ibfk_1   | departments           | department_id
## employees      | manager_id    | employees_ibfk_2   | employees             | employee_id
## leave_requests | approved_by   | leave_requests_ibfk_3 | employees          | employee_id
## leave_requests | employee_id   | leave_requests_ibfk_1 | employees          | employee_id
leave_requests | leave_type_id | leave_requests_ibfk_2 | leave_types        | leave_type_id
## payroll        | employee_id   | payroll_ibfk_1     | employees             | employee_id

Seven relationships, matching the design. A missing line would be a finding. To check whether the constraints are trusted:
```sql
-- PostgreSQL: convalidated = false means NOT VALID (existing rows never checked)
SELECT conname, conrelid::regclass AS table_name, convalidated
FROM   pg_constraint WHERE contype = 'f';
```

```sql
-- SQL Server: disabled or untrusted foreign keys
SELECT name, OBJECT_NAME(parent_object_id) AS table_name, is_disabled, is_not_trusted
FROM   sys.foreign_keys;
```

```sql
-- MySQL: are checks currently on for this session? (1 = on)
SELECT @@foreign_key_checks;
```

Any is_disabled = 1, is_not_trusted = 1 or convalidated = false is worth raising. To repair an untrusted constraint, the DBA re-validates it (WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT in SQL Server, VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in PostgreSQL), and the check fails until the orphans are cleaned up, which is a handy way to confirm your orphan queries are right.
To hunt for missing foreign keys, list columns that look like references (named something_id, not primary keys) and have no FK:

| -- MySQL | SELECT c.table_name, c.column_name | FROM   information_schema.columns c | LEFT JOIN information_schema.key_column_usage k | ON  k.table_schema = c.table_schema AND k.table_name = c.table_name |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AND k.column_name  = c.column_name  AND k.referenced_table_name IS NOT NULL | WHERE  c.table_schema = 'hrms_practice' | AND  c.column_name LIKE '%\_id' | AND  c.column_key <> 'PRI' | AND  k.column_name IS NULL; |

For our schema this returns nothing, since every _id reference is constrained. Note that it also wouldn't catch approved_by, which references an employee but doesn't end in _id. Naming heuristics find candidates, not proof, so ask developers for any references the database can't see.
## Step 2: find orphans with anti-joins
For every FK-shaped relationship, ask "which child rows point at a parent that isn't there?" using the anti-join from 4.1. The one-line-per-relationship version below is worth saving as a reusable script, since it produces a scoreboard for the whole schema:
```sql
SELECT 'employees.department_id' AS relationship, COUNT(*) AS orphans
FROM   employees e LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
WHERE  e.department_id IS NOT NULL AND d.department_id IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'employees.manager_id', COUNT(*)
FROM   employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
WHERE  e.manager_id IS NOT NULL AND m.employee_id IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'leave_requests.employee_id', COUNT(*)
FROM   leave_requests lr LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = lr.employee_id
WHERE  e.employee_id IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'leave_requests.leave_type_id', COUNT(*)
FROM   leave_requests lr LEFT JOIN leave_types lt ON lt.leave_type_id = lr.leave_type_id
WHERE  lt.leave_type_id IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'leave_requests.approved_by', COUNT(*)
FROM   leave_requests lr LEFT JOIN employees a ON a.employee_id = lr.approved_by
WHERE  lr.approved_by IS NOT NULL AND a.employee_id IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'attendance.employee_id', COUNT(*)
FROM   attendance at LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = at.employee_id
WHERE  e.employee_id IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'payroll.employee_id', COUNT(*)
FROM   payroll p LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = p.employee_id
WHERE  e.employee_id IS NULL;
```

| relationship                  \| orphans | employees.department_id       \| 1 | employees.manager_id          \| 0 | leave_requests.employee_id    \| 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| leave_requests.leave_type_id  \| 0 | leave_requests.approved_by    \| 0 | attendance.employee_id        \| 0 | payroll.employee_id           \| 1 |

The three non-zero rows are exactly the three orphans we planted. In a real project, a run that prints all zeros is your evidence for a data-integrity sign-off, and anything else is a defect with a ready-made reproduction. Notice the IS NOT NULL guards on the nullable columns (department_id, manager_id, approved_by). Without them, every legitimately blank reference would be reported as an orphan. Mandatory columns don't need the guard, and adding it is harmless.
To see the offending rows rather than a count (for the bug report), drop the aggregation:
```sql
SELECT lr.leave_request_id, lr.employee_id, lr.status, lr.start_date
FROM   leave_requests lr
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = lr.employee_id
WHERE  e.employee_id IS NULL;
```

leave_request_id | employee_id | status   | start_date
10               | 99          | approved | 2026-11-02

## Step 3: find logical orphans (the parent exists but shouldn't count)
Foreign keys can't see the soft-delete flag or the employee status. You have to encode that rule yourself. Here it's "pending leave belonging to someone who is no longer active", the data left behind by an offboarding flow that didn't clean up after itself:
```sql
SELECT lr.leave_request_id, lr.employee_id, lr.status AS leave_status,
       e.status AS employee_status, e.is_deleted
```
| FROM   leave_requests lr | JOIN   employees e ON e.employee_id = lr.employee_id |
|---|---|
| WHERE  lr.status = 'pending' | AND  (e.is_deleted = 1 OR e.status <> 'active'); |

leave_request_id | employee_id | leave_status | employee_status | is_deleted
11               | 5           | pending      | inactive        | 1

A pending request for a deactivated employee will sit in a manager's approval queue forever, or worse, get approved and count against payroll. The same pattern applies to payroll rows for resigned employees, attendance after the last working day, and approvals whose approver has left. Whether each is a defect depends on the requirement, but the query gives you the evidence to ask. The relationship rule "approver isn't the requester" is a similar check that no constraint enforces: SELECT * FROM leave_requests WHERE approved_by = employee_id.
## Step 4: check expected children that are missing
Orphans are children without parents. The mirror problem is parents that should have children but don't. Which active employees have no payroll for August 2026?
```sql
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.hire_date
FROM   employees e
LEFT JOIN payroll p ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id AND p.pay_month = '2026-08-01'
WHERE  e.status = 'active' AND e.is_deleted = 0
  AND  p.payroll_id IS NULL;
```

employee_id | first_name | hire_date
6           | Puja       | 2026-08-15
7           | Tenzing    | 2026-09-01

The month condition sits in the ON clause, so the outer join still reports employees with no August row (see 4.1). Tenzing was hired on 1 September, so no August payroll is expected, and adding AND e.hire_date < '2026-09-01' removes him. Puja was hired mid-August, so whether she needs a prorated August payslip is a business rule for you to confirm. This "who is missing" query is the backbone of completeness checks: every active employee has a payroll row for the closed month, every approved leave has a balance movement, every booked appointment has a ledger entry.
## Step 5: check cardinality (one-to-many that should have been one-to-one)
Some relationships must be exactly one-to-one in practice: one payroll row per employee per month, one attendance row per employee per day. If the "one" side has duplicates, joins fan out (4.1) and totals inflate. Check the counts directly:
```sql
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, COUNT(*) AS payroll_rows
```
| FROM   employees e | JOIN   payroll p ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id AND p.pay_month = '2026-08-01' |
|---|---|
| GROUP  BY e.employee_id, e.first_name | HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; |

employee_id | first_name | payroll_rows
2           | Ravi       | 2

That's the duplicate payroll row from Part 3, found through the relationship this time. The root cause is a missing UNIQUE (employee_id, pay_month) constraint, which is worth reporting alongside the data defect: cleaning the row doesn't stop the next duplicate.
## Step 6: test that the constraints really fire (behaviour tests)
Finding zero orphans today doesn't prove the database will reject one tomorrow. Try to break each rule inside a transaction that you roll back (0.4). You expect these errors:
```sql
START TRANSACTION;
```

-- Child pointing at a parent that doesn't exist
```sql
INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days)
VALUES (999, 1, '2026-12-01', '2026-12-01', 1);
-- MySQL:      ERROR 1452 (23000): Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails
-- PostgreSQL: ERROR: insert or update on table "leave_requests" violates foreign key constraint "leave_requests_employee_id_fkey"
-- SQL Server: Msg 547: The INSERT statement conflicted with the FOREIGN KEY constraint ...
```

-- Deleting a parent that still has children
```sql
DELETE FROM departments WHERE department_id = 2;
-- MySQL:      ERROR 1451 (23000): Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails
-- PostgreSQL: ERROR: update or delete on table "departments" violates foreign key constraint "employees_department_id_fkey" on table "employees"
-- SQL Server: Msg 547: The DELETE statement conflicted with the REFERENCE constraint ...
```

```sql
ROLLBACK;
```

If the second statement succeeds and your QA employees are left with a dangling department_id, the constraint is missing or disabled. What the delete does depends on the referential action chosen for the constraint:

| Action | What happens to children when the parent is deleted | Test focus | RESTRICT / NO ACTION (default) | Delete is blocked with an error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| UI must show a friendly message, not a raw error or a 500 | CASCADE | Children are deleted too | Confirm this is intended, since a cascade from departments to employees would wipe out staff | SET NULL |
| Child's FK becomes NULL (column must allow it) | Do screens cope with NULL (an employee with no department)? | SET DEFAULT | Child's FK becomes the default value (not in MySQL InnoDB) | Does the default parent exist? |

Then repeat the check from the application layer. Try deleting a department that has employees through the UI and API. The good outcome is a clear message and unchanged data; the bad outcomes are a generic server error, a "success" message with the department still in place, or a cascade nobody expected. A Playwright version:
```ts
test('cannot delete a department that still has employees', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/departments');
  await page.getByRole('row', { name: /QA/ }).getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm' }).click();
```

  await expect(page.getByText(/employees are still assigned/i)).toBeVisible();   // friendly message

```ts
  const [rows]: any = await db.execute(
    "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM departments WHERE name = 'QA'");
  expect(rows[0].n).toBe(1);                                                      // still there
  const [orph]: any = await db.execute(`
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM employees e
    LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
    WHERE e.department_id IS NOT NULL AND d.department_id IS NULL`);
  expect(orph[0].n).toBe(1);   // only the pre-existing orphan (Tenzing); no NEW orphans
});
```

Make assertions about deltas (no new orphans), not absolute zero, on a shared database that already contains known bad rows. The equivalent in Selenium is the same steps with driver.find_element(...) and a database cursor.
## Step 7: soft delete and the app's own cleanup
For "deletes" that only set is_deleted = 1, the database won't stop anything, so the app itself must handle the children. After deactivating or deleting an employee in the UI, run the logical-orphan queries from Step 3. Ask what should happen to pending leave (cancelled?), future attendance, payroll for the current cycle, direct reports (reassigned?) and approvals in progress. Then check each in the database. This is where offboarding and status-change workflows most often leave data behind.
## Step 8: turn the checks into a reusable suite
Put the scoreboard query, the logical-orphan queries and the completeness queries in one file, each with a comment that says what a non-empty result means. Run it after every migration, import, data fix, environment refresh and major release, and add it to the pipeline as a sanity stage (9.4). Each check stays cheap and deterministic, and a failing one names the exact relationship and rows, which is why they're some of the highest-value tests you can add. Chapter 6.3 extends these into duplicate and mismatched-count detection, and 10.2 turns them into a maintained library.
## Writing up an integrity bug
A good report includes the relationship (leave_requests.employee_id → employees.employee_id), the query that finds the orphans, the count and a few example IDs, the environment and time you ran it, how the data probably got there (import, deleted parent, disabled checks), and the visible impact (missing row in a report, error on opening a screen, wrong totals). Attach the result as a CSV (11.3). Severity depends on what the row feeds: an orphan in an audit log is annoying, while an orphan in payroll is a money problem.
## Cleanup: put the sample database back
Run the preview first and delete only the rows Part 4 created (the safe workflow from 0.4):
```sql
SELECT leave_request_id FROM leave_requests WHERE leave_request_id IN (10, 11);   -- preview
```

```sql
DELETE FROM leave_requests WHERE leave_request_id IN (10, 11);
DELETE FROM payroll        WHERE payroll_id = 8;
DELETE FROM employees      WHERE employee_id IN (6, 7);
DELETE FROM leave_types    WHERE name = 'Unpaid';
DELETE FROM departments    WHERE name = 'Legal';
```

Auto-increment counters don't roll back, so the next inserted rows will get higher IDs than before. Part 6 re-adds its own defects in a setup block when it needs them.
